How Genetic Modification Really Works

This module builds the science you need before any debate makes sense: what DNA, genes and proteins do, how scientists move one gene into a crop, and which traits GM crops actually carry. You finish by sorting the claims you have heard into clear types so you know which evidence each one needs.

Every living thing, from a cowpea plant to a goat to the yeast that raises your bread, carries a set of instructions written in **DNA**. DNA is a long chain made of four chemical letters, usually written **A, T, G and C**. The order of these letters is the message. A stretch of DNA that carries the instructions for one job is called a **gene**.
A twisted DNA double helix
DNA is the instruction book; a gene is one recipe inside it.

Most genes are recipes for **proteins**. Proteins do the work in a cell. Some proteins build structures, some speed up chemical reactions, some carry signals. The colour of a maize grain, a cowpea's ability to fix nitrogen, or a plant's response to drought all come from proteins made from genes, working together with the environment the plant grows in.

What makes an organism genetically modified

The World Health Organization (WHO) defines genetically modified organisms (GMOs) as organisms, meaning plants, animals or microorganisms, in which the DNA has been altered **in a way that does not occur naturally by mating and/or natural recombination**. The key idea is the method. When two cowpea plants cross in a field, their genes mix, but that is natural mating, so the offspring is not a GMO. When a scientist inserts a chosen gene into a cowpea cell in a laboratory, the result is a GMO.

This also explains why a GMO can carry a gene from a very different living thing. Mating can only mix genes between closely related plants. Laboratory methods can move a gene from a soil bacterium into a plant, because DNA uses the same four letters in all living things, and the plant cell can read a bacterial recipe once it is placed correctly.
Traditional and modern biotechnology

**Biotechnology** simply means using living things or their parts to make products. By that meaning, Nigerian women have practised biotechnology for generations. **Modern biotechnology** is the newer set of laboratory tools that work directly on DNA, such as recombinant DNA (joining DNA from different sources) and genome editing. Regulators, including Nigeria's biosafety law, focus on modern biotechnology and its products.

Many people are surprised to learn that GM products already sit quietly in daily life. Human insulin used by many people with diabetes is made by genetically modified microorganisms that carry the human insulin gene. Much of the cheese made around the world uses an enzyme called chymosin produced by GM microbes instead of taking it from calves' stomachs. These uses rarely cause public argument, which shows that the debate is usually about particular crops, companies and decisions, not about the science of DNA itself.
Worked example: sorting products into the right category
For example, Amaka, a secondary school biology teacher in Enugu, prepares a short sorting exercise for her women's group before a discussion on GM foods.
She lists six items: ogi, yoghurt, seed she selected from her best cowpea plants, human insulin, cheese made with microbial chymosin, and an insect-resistant GM cowpea.
She asks for each item: did people change the DNA directly in a laboratory? If no, it is traditional biotechnology or ordinary breeding.
Ogi, yoghurt and selected seed answer no: 3 items are traditional.
Insulin, microbial chymosin and GM cowpea answer yes: 3 items come from modern biotechnology.
She points out that only one of the 3 modern items is a living crop planted in fields, which is why it faces environmental review as well as food review.
The group sees that 3 of 6 everyday items involve modern biotechnology, and that the method of change, not the name of the food, decides the category.
Hybrid is not the same as GM

Hybrid seed comes from crossing two chosen parent lines by pollination. No gene is inserted in a laboratory, so a hybrid is not a GMO. A GM variety can also be a hybrid if the inserted gene is bred into hybrid parents, so always ask how the variety was made.

Keep this lesson's core idea in mind for the whole course. A GMO is defined by **how** its DNA was changed. Whether a particular GMO is safe, useful, fairly priced or legal to plant are separate questions, and each needs its own evidence. The rest of this course gives you the tools to answer each one carefully.

Making a GM crop is slow, careful work that usually takes many years from the first idea to seed in a farmer's hand. This lesson walks through the main steps using the best-known example in Africa: crops that carry a gene from the soil bacterium ***Bacillus thuringiensis***, shortened to **Bt**.
A woman scientist looking into a microscope
Plant transformation happens in single cells grown in the laboratory before any plant reaches a field.
Step 1: choose the gene

Bt bacteria make proteins called **Cry proteins**. A Cry protein is harmless to most animals, but when a specific group of insect larvae eat it, the protein is activated in their gut, binds to particular receptors on the gut wall and damages it, so the larva stops feeding and dies. Each Cry protein affects a narrow group of insects. Bt sprays made from the bacteria have long been used by farmers, including organic farmers. In a Bt crop, the plant itself makes the Cry protein, so the larva meets it when it bites the plant.

For example, Nigeria's biosafety regulator has published an application for a GM cowpea containing the **Cry2Ab** gene, which gives resistance to the **Maruca pod borer**, a caterpillar that bores into cowpea flowers and pods.
Step 2: build the gene construct

A gene on its own does nothing in a new organism. Scientists join it to control signals. The **promoter** is the on-switch that tells the plant where and how strongly to use the gene. The **trait gene** is the recipe itself, often adjusted so the plant reads it efficiently. A **marker gene** lets scientists find the few cells that took up the construct. This whole package is the **construct**.

Each step filters out failures, so only a few plants from thousands of cells go forward.
Step 3: transform plant cells

**Agrobacterium method:** *Agrobacterium tumefaciens* is a soil bacterium that naturally transfers a piece of its DNA into plant cells. Scientists remove the disease-causing genes and use it as a delivery vehicle for the construct.
**Gene gun (biolistics):** tiny gold or tungsten particles coated with DNA are fired into plant tissue, and some cells take the DNA into their own.
After either method, the cells are grown on a nutrient gel (tissue culture). The marker helps keep only transformed cells, which are regrown into whole plants.

Each time the construct lands in a plant's DNA, it lands in one particular place. That single, specific insertion is called an **event**. Different events of the same gene can behave differently, so developers compare many events and keep the one with stable, useful expression and no obvious side effects. Regulators approve a named event, not a gene in general. That is why the Nigerian cowpea application refers to **Event 245F**.
Step 4: breed the trait into varieties farmers want

The event is usually first made in a variety that is easy to transform, not the variety farmers prefer. Breeders then use **backcrossing**: they cross the GM plant with a popular local variety, select offspring carrying the gene, cross those back to the local variety again, and repeat. Each backcross halves the share of DNA still coming from the transformation parent.
Worked example: how many backcrosses are needed?
For example, a breeding team wants a GM cowpea line that is at least 95 percent the same as a local variety farmers already like for its grain colour and cooking quality.
First cross (GM line x local variety): on average 50 percent of the DNA comes from the local variety.
Backcross 1: half of the remaining 50 percent is replaced, so 50 + 25 = 75 percent local.
Backcross 2: 75 + 12.5 = 87.5 percent local.
Backcross 3: 87.5 + 6.25 = 93.75 percent local, still below 95.
Backcross 4: 93.75 + 3.125 = 96.875 percent local, which passes the 95 percent goal.
At each generation they keep only plants that still carry the Bt gene, checked with a laboratory test.
Four backcrosses after the first cross give about 96.9 percent local DNA on average. With one cowpea generation per season, this is one reason GM varieties take years to reach farmers.
Genome editing is a different tool

**Genome editing**, for example with **CRISPR-Cas9**, works like a find-and-replace tool. A guide molecule finds an exact spot in the plant's own DNA and an enzyme cuts it there. When the cell repairs the cut, a few letters can be changed, switched off or replaced. Often no foreign gene remains in the final plant. Because of this, countries are still deciding how to treat edited crops: some regulate them like GMOs, some treat certain edits like conventional breeding. Always check the current rule in your own country rather than assuming.
Never plant seed of unknown origin

Seed passed hand to hand and described as a new improved or GM variety may be unapproved, mislabelled or fake. Planting unapproved GM material is against the law in countries with biosafety laws, and fake seed can ruin a season. Buy only labelled, certified seed from registered dealers.

In Nigeria, the National Biosafety Management Agency (NBMA) has published notices about insect-resistant cowpea and about **TELA maize**, which it described as resistant to fall armyworm and stem borer and tolerant of drought. These crops target pests that Nigerian farmers already fight with repeated spraying or heavy losses. Whether a particular variety is approved and on sale in your area at a given time is something you check with NBMA and your extension office, not something to assume.

Notice that a trait solves one named problem, not every problem. A Bt cowpea that resists Maruca pod borer still needs protection from other pests, good spacing, weeding and proper drying after harvest. A drought-tolerant maize still yields less in a drought than in a good season; it simply tends to lose less. When someone describes a GM crop as a complete answer, ask which pest or stress it targets and what it leaves untouched.

Also remember that the same trait can be placed in many different crops and varieties, and that the event, the variety and the country all matter. A trait that has been approved in one country may not be approved in its neighbour, and an event approved for food import may not be approved for planting.
Four types of claim

Most confusion comes from mixing up different kinds of question. Someone may say "GMOs are bad" when they really mean "I am worried big seed companies will control farmers". That is a real concern, but it is an economic question, not a food safety question. Answering it with food safety evidence, or the other way round, goes nowhere.
Four kinds of GMO claim
Food safety: is it safe to eat?
Environment: effects on insects, weeds, wild plants
Economics: cost, yield, seed control
Law and policy: approved, labelled, regulated?
About people or about the wider system
About health or about money and rules
Each type of claim needs a different kind of evidence and a different expert.
**Food safety claims** need evidence from food safety assessments and health bodies such as WHO and Codex.
**Environmental claims** need field studies and environmental risk assessments for that crop in that place.
**Economic claims** need farm records, seed prices, yield data and market information.
**Legal and policy claims** need the actual law and the regulator's published decisions.

Evidence, Risk and Regulation

This module looks at the evidence behind the three biggest questions: is GM food safe to eat, what happens in the field and on the farm, and who decides what may be planted. You will learn how food safety assessment works, the real environmental and economic issues, and how international rules and Nigeria's biosafety law fit together.

When people ask "Is GM food safe?", scientists answer with a narrower question: **is this particular food, from this particular event, as safe as the conventional food it replaces?** That question can be tested. It is the basis of international guidance agreed by governments through the **Codex Alimentarius Commission**, the joint body of the Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO) and WHO that sets international food standards.
A test tube with liquid
Food safety assessment compares the GM food with its conventional counterpart, one property at a time.
The six areas WHO lists
WHO explains that safety assessment of GM foods generally looks at:
**Toxicity:** direct health effects of the new protein or any changed substances.
**Allergenicity:** whether the food could provoke an allergic reaction.
**Specific components** thought to have nutritional or toxic properties.
**Stability of the inserted gene** over generations.
**Nutritional effects** linked to the modification.
**Unintended effects:** any change nobody planned, found by comparing the GM and conventional plant.
The comparative approach

Codex guideline CXG 45-2003, on food safety assessment of foods from recombinant-DNA plants, uses a **comparator**: the conventional version of the same crop with a history of safe use. Developers grow the GM plant and its comparator side by side and measure nutrients, natural toxins and anti-nutrients. Differences are then examined: is the difference large, is it outside the normal range seen in ordinary varieties, and could it affect health?
Comparative safety assessment
Pick the conventional comparator
Grow both side by side
Measure composition and new protein
Investigate any real difference
Decide: as safe or not
Every difference found sends the assessor back to look more closely before a decision is made.

For the new protein itself, assessors check whether it resembles known toxins or allergens, how quickly it breaks down in digestion-like conditions, and how much of it is present in the part people eat. Eating DNA is not a risk in itself: people eat the DNA of every plant and animal in their diet daily, and digestion breaks it down. The question is always what the new protein and any unintended changes do.
Worked example: reading a compositional comparison

For example, a study summary for an illustrative GM cowpea lists protein content per 100 g of dry grain for the GM line, its conventional comparator, and the range found across many ordinary cowpea varieties. The numbers below are for practice only.
GM line: 24.1 g protein. Comparator: 23.5 g protein. Normal range in ordinary varieties: 20.0 to 28.0 g.
Difference: 24.1 minus 23.5 = 0.6 g.
Percentage difference: 0.6 divided by 23.5 = 0.0255, about 2.6 percent.
Check the range: 24.1 lies between 20.0 and 28.0, so it is normal for cowpea.
Now suppose a natural anti-nutrient were 40 percent higher and outside the normal range. That would need explanation and possibly more testing before approval.
A 2.6 percent difference inside the normal range is not a safety concern on its own. Assessors care about differences that are large, outside natural variation or biologically meaningful.

Allergy checks deserve special attention because allergies can be severe. Assessors ask whether the gene came from a source known to cause allergies, whether the new protein's sequence resembles any known allergen, and whether it survives digestion. If a protein raised a real allergy concern, the product would not be expected to pass, which is the purpose of checking before release rather than after.
What WHO actually concludes

WHO's public guidance states that **GM foods currently available on the international market have passed safety assessments and are not likely to present risks for human health**. Read the sentence carefully. It covers foods that have passed assessment. It does not say every possible GM food is safe, and WHO adds that each GM food should be assessed case by case. That is exactly why assessment and regulation exist.

Whether a grain is GM or not, the everyday hazards remain: mould and aflatoxin in badly dried maize and groundnuts, pesticide residues when spraying rules are ignored, and weevil-damaged grain. Dry grain well, store it off the floor in clean bags, and never eat seed that has been treated with chemicals.

Food safety is only one part of the GMO question. The more open debates, and the ones that matter most to farmers, are about what happens in the field and in the farm account book. These are real issues, and a balanced person can discuss them without exaggeration in either direction.
A ladybird beetle
Environmental review asks how a GM crop affects insects it was not designed to target.
Resistance: the trait can wear out

Insects and weeds evolve. If a field of Bt plants kills almost every pod borer, the rare larva that carries a natural resistance gene survives, mates with another survivor and passes resistance on. Within some seasons the trait stops working. Insect resistance to Bt crops and weed resistance to herbicides have been reported in several countries where stewardship was weak. WHO also lists effects on non-target organisms and gene escape among the environmental issues assessed.

The main defence for Bt crops is a **refuge**: an area of non-Bt plants of the same crop planted near the Bt field. Susceptible insects survive in the refuge and mate with any rare resistant insects from the Bt field, so their offspring stay susceptible. The refuge size and layout are set in the stewardship guide that comes with the seed, so always follow that guide.
How a refuge slows resistance
Bt field kills most larvae
Rare resistant survivors emerge
Refuge produces many susceptible insects
They mate with survivors
Offspring stay susceptible
Without the refuge, survivors mate with each other and resistance builds quickly.
Worked example: planning a refuge

For example, Ngozi farms 2 hectares in Benue and buys certified Bt cowpea seed. Suppose the stewardship leaflet with her seed says 20 percent of her cowpea area must be refuge planted with non-Bt cowpea. The 20 percent is used here only for practice; her real figure comes from her own leaflet.
Total cowpea area: 2 hectares = 20,000 square metres.
Refuge: 20 percent of 20,000 = 0.20 x 20,000 = 4,000 square metres.
Bt area: 20,000 minus 4,000 = 16,000 square metres.
Her field is 100 m wide, so a refuge strip along one side is 4,000 divided by 100 = 40 m deep.
She marks the strip with pegs before planting and writes the layout in her farm notebook.
Ngozi plants 16,000 square metres of Bt cowpea and a 40 m by 100 m strip (4,000 square metres) of non-Bt cowpea as refuge.

Stewardship is a shared job. One farmer who skips the refuge weakens the trait for every neighbour growing the same crop, because insects fly between farms. This is why cooperatives and extension officers often discuss refuge rules as a group, and why a farmer who buys GM seed should read and keep the stewardship leaflet as carefully as the seed label.
Gene flow and seed saving

Pollen moves by wind and insects. **Gene flow** is when pollen from a GM crop fertilises a neighbouring plant, either a non-GM field of the same crop or a wild relative. Risk assessors ask whether the crop has wild relatives in the area, whether the trait would give those relatives an advantage, and how far pollen travels. These are local questions, which is why environmental assessment is done country by country. Gene flow also matters to farmers who save seed or sell to buyers that demand non-GM grain.
The farm account book

Economic claims cut both ways. GM seed may cost more, may come with stewardship rules, and in some systems is sold under licence. On the other hand, an insect-resistant crop can need fewer insecticide sprays, which saves chemical, labour and the farmer's own exposure to poison. The honest answer depends on the actual seed price, pest pressure and spraying practice on that farm.

No single world authority approves GM crops. Instead, international agreements set shared principles, and each country's own law and regulator decide what may be imported, tested or planted. Knowing which body does what lets you check claims about the law quickly and accurately.
A woman holding the scales of justice
Biosafety law balances potential benefits against possible risks to health and the environment.
The international layer

**Cartagena Protocol on Biosafety:** adopted on 29 January 2000 as a supplementary agreement to the Convention on Biological Diversity. It aims to protect biological diversity from potential risks of living modified organisms from modern biotechnology. It sets an **advance informed agreement** procedure, so a country gets the information it needs before agreeing to import such organisms, and it created the **Biosafety Clearing-House**, an online system for sharing information.

**Codex Alimentarius:** the joint FAO and WHO food standards body. Its texts include CXG 44-2003, Principles for the Risk Analysis of Foods Derived from Modern Biotechnology, and CXG 45-2003 on safety assessment of foods from recombinant-DNA plants, plus a compilation of texts relevant to labelling.
**Labelling:** WHO notes there is no worldwide consensus on labelling and traceability of GM foods, so rules differ from country to country.
The Nigerian layer

In Nigeria, the regulator is the **National Biosafety Management Agency (NBMA)**, established under the National Biosafety Management Agency Act, signed in April 2015. The agency describes its mandate as providing a regulatory framework to safeguard human health and the environment from potential adverse effects of modern biotechnology and its products, while harnessing their potential for the benefit of Nigerians. It regulates the release into the environment, handling and use of GMOs, and it acts against unauthorised material: for example, it has publicised the disposal of unauthorised transgenic cotton seed.

The Act requires **public display** of applications for permits to intentionally release a GMO, so citizens can give input before a decision. In April 2023, for example, NBMA displayed the application by the **Institute of Agricultural Research (IAR), Samaru, Zaria** for general release of GM cowpea Event 245F with the Cry2Ab gene for Maruca pod borer resistance. The notice ran for 21 days, from 6 to 26 April 2023, and asked for comments to be sent to the Director-General by email.

Worked example: planning a comment on a display notice

For example, Funmi chairs a farmers' cooperative in Ogun. A new notice appears on the NBMA website with a 21-day display that opens on a Monday, 3 March. She wants the cooperative's comment in on time.
Day 1 is 3 March, so day 21 is 3 + 20 = 23 March. That is the last day to submit.
She sets an internal deadline 3 days earlier, 20 March, to allow for network problems.
Week 1 (3 to 9 March): she downloads the notice and reads the summary with two members.
Week 2 (10 to 16 March): the cooperative meets and writes its questions, for example on refuge rules and seed availability.

Week 3 (17 to 20 March): she types a short, polite comment naming the application, the cooperative and its specific questions, and sends it to the email address in the notice, keeping a screenshot of the sent message.
The comment is sent on 20 March, three days before the 23 March deadline, with a clear record of what was sent and when.
How to write a useful comment

A comment is most useful when it is specific and polite. Name the application exactly as it appears in the notice. Say who you are, for example a cooperative of cowpea growers. Then ask clear questions or raise concerns that the regulator can act on, such as how refuge rules will be explained to smallholders, where certified seed will be sold, or how farmers will report problems. Avoid general statements such as "we reject GMOs" or "we support science" with no reasons, because they give the reviewers nothing to examine.

Keep a copy of everything you send, and note the date and time. If you receive a reply, file it with your notes. This record shows your group took part in the process and helps you follow the decision when it is published.
Check the source, then check the date

Approval status changes. Before you repeat a claim about what is approved or banned, look for the regulator's own notice and note its date. Use the NBMA website for Nigeria and the Biosafety Clearing-House for other countries that are Parties to the Protocol.

Other agencies also play roles around GM products in Nigeria, for example in seed certification and food registration. When you are unsure which body handles a question, ask NBMA or your state agricultural extension office directly and write down the answer, the person and the date.

In Module 1 you started a claims log. Now you will test those claims with one repeatable method. The aim is not to win arguments. It is to reach a fair verdict you can explain, and to be honest when the answer is "partly true" or "not yet known".
A magnifying glass
Every claim gets the same five questions, whichever side it favours.
The five questions
Five questions for any claim
What exactly is claimed?
Which type of claim?
Who is the source?
What evidence is shown?
Is it about here and now?
Score each question 0, 1 or 2, for a total out of 10.
**What exactly is claimed?** Rewrite it as one clear sentence. Vague claims such as "GMOs are poison" do not name a crop, event or effect. Score 2 if specific, 1 if partly, 0 if vague.
**Which type?** Food safety, environment, economics or law. Score 2 if the evidence offered matches the type, 0 if it does not, for example a seed price used to prove a health danger.

**Who is the source?** Score 2 for a regulator, WHO, FAO, Codex or a named peer-reviewed study, 1 for a named expert or reputable news report that cites one, 0 for an anonymous forward or a seller of a competing product.
**What evidence is shown?** Score 2 if you can follow it to the original document, 1 if it is described but not linked, 0 if none.
**Here and now?** Score 2 if it concerns an approved product in your country and is current, 1 if it is from elsewhere or old, 0 if it describes something not present here.
A total of 8 to 10 suggests a credible claim, 4 to 7 means partly supported and needs more checking, and 0 to 3 means do not repeat it. The score guides your judgement; it does not replace it.
Worked example: scoring two claims fairly
For example, Chioma, a nurse in Port Harcourt, scores two messages from her church WhatsApp group: one against GMOs and one in favour.

Claim 1: "GM foods cause cancer, a doctor said so." Specific? Partly, no crop named: 1. Type match? No evidence offered of any kind: 0. Source? An unnamed doctor: 0. Evidence? None: 0. Here and now? Not linked to any product in Nigeria: 0. Total: 1 + 0 + 0 + 0 + 0 = 1 out of 10.

Claim 2: "GM cowpea will end hunger in Nigeria." Specific? Names a crop but 'end hunger' is vague: 1. Type match? An economic and food security claim with no yield or price data: 0. Source? A seed advert: 0. Evidence? None: 0. Here and now? Relates to a crop discussed by Nigeria's regulator: 2. Total: 1 + 0 + 0 + 0 + 2 = 3 out of 10.
She compares both with WHO's statement on approved GM foods and with NBMA's published notices.

She writes a verdict for each: Claim 1 is not supported by WHO's assessment of approved foods. Claim 2 overstates what one pest-resistance trait can do; hunger also depends on prices, storage, income and conflict.
Both claims score 3 or less, so Chioma does not forward either. She posts one calm message with WHO's statement and a link to NBMA's website.

Use the score honestly when you like the conclusion. It is tempting to give a friendly claim an extra point. If you notice yourself doing this, score the claim again as if it came from someone you disagree with.

Facts alone rarely change minds. People hold views on food because they care about their children's health, their money and their land. A good facilitator respects that care first, then helps the group look at evidence together. This lesson gives you a plan you can run in a cooperative meeting, a church women's fellowship or a market association.
People sitting together in a group discussion
A balanced conversation lets people voice concerns before evidence is shared.
Three principles
**Listen before you explain.** Ask what people have heard and what worries them. Write their concerns where all can see.
**Sort before you answer.** Group concerns into the four types: food safety, environment, economics, law. Many arguments disappear once people see they are talking about different questions.

**Say what is settled and what is open.** Settled: WHO's position on approved GM foods, the fact that Nigeria has a biosafety regulator. Open: whether a particular variety will pay on a particular farm, how well stewardship will be followed, how seed supply will work over time.

For example, Grace leads the monthly meeting of a 25-member women farmers' cooperative in Plateau. She has 30 minutes on the agenda.

Before the session

Preparation matters as much as the meeting itself. Agree the time slot with the group's leader so you are not squeezed into the last five minutes. Print your handout the day before. Check the NBMA website again so your facts are current, and write the date you checked on the handout. If you plan to invite an extension officer or a teacher, confirm in writing and tell them which questions the group is likely to ask.

Think about language and setting too. In many groups, a session in Hausa, Igbo, Yoruba, Pidgin or another local language will reach more people than one in English. Choose simple words for technical terms, for example "a gene is one recipe in the plant's instruction book". Seat people in a circle if you can, so it feels like a conversation rather than a lecture.

Write every concern on the flip chart in the speaker's own words, then ask the group to help place each one under food safety, environment, economics or law. When you share facts, read WHO's sentence aloud exactly as written and show NBMA's website on your phone. When you reach open questions, invite people who farm to speak first, because they know the local pest pressure, costs and seed supply better than anyone.

Some people will keep their view, and that is their right. Your goal is that they know where to check facts and that the group can discuss the topic without hostility. Why this matters
Science first, then the debate
What DNA, genes and proteins do
How one gene is moved into a crop
Which traits GM crops carry
How to sort the claims you hear
Before any debate about GMOs makes sense, you need the science. In this video you will see what genes do, and how scientists move one gene into a crop.
Then you will learn which traits GM crops really carry, and how to sort the claims you hear so you know what evidence each one needs.
The basics
DNA: four letters, A, T, G and C
Gene: one recipe, a stretch of DNA
Protein: made from the recipe
Trait: what you see in the plant
Every living thing, from a cowpea plant to the yeast in your bread, carries instructions written in DNA. DNA uses four chemical letters, A, T, G and C. Their order is the message.
A stretch of DNA that carries the instructions for one job is a gene.
Most genes are recipes for proteins. Proteins do the work in a cell.
The colour of a maize grain, or a plant's response to drought, comes from proteins working with the environment. Change the letters, and you can change the trait.
Biotechnology
Traditional or modern?
Traditional
Fermenting ogi or garri
Making yoghurt, raising bread
Selecting the best seed to replant
No direct change to DNA
Modern
DNA changed in a laboratory
Insulin made by GM microbes
Insect-resistant Bt crops
Genome editing such as CRISPR
Biotechnology simply means using living things to make products. By that meaning, Nigerian women have practised it for generations, fermenting ogi and selecting the best seed.
Modern biotechnology works directly on DNA in a laboratory. The World Health Organization defines a GMO by the method: DNA altered in a way that does not occur naturally by mating.
So when two cowpea plants cross in a field, that is not a GMO. And a hybrid is not a GMO either, because no gene is inserted.
Step by step
Never plant seed of unknown origin. Buy certified seed.
Choose the trait gene
Build the gene construct

The best-known example in Africa is Bt. The soil bacterium Bacillus thuringiensis makes Cry proteins, which kill a narrow group of insect larvae that eat them. For example, a GM cowpea carries a gene that resists the Maruca pod borer.
Scientists join the gene to a promoter, the on-switch, and a marker gene that helps find the cells that took it up. This package is the construct.
They deliver it with Agrobacterium, a soil bacterium that naturally transfers DNA into plants, or with a gene gun.
Each insertion lands in one place, called an event. Developers compare many events and keep the best. Regulators approve a named event, such as Event 245F.
Finally breeders cross the trait into a local variety farmers like. This takes years.
Seed passed hand to hand as a new GM variety may be unapproved or fake. Planting unapproved GM material is against the law where there are biosafety laws.
Worked example
Backcrossing to a local variety
First cross: 50 percent local DNA
Backcross 1: 75 percent
Backcross 2: 87.5 percent
Backcross 3: 93.75 percent
Backcross 4: 96.875 percent, goal met
For example, a team wants a GM cowpea at least 95 percent the same as a local variety. The first cross gives 50 percent local DNA.
Each backcross halves what is left from the GM parent. 75, then 87.5, then 93.75. Still below 95.
The fourth backcross gives about 96.9 percent. With one cowpea generation a season, this is one reason GM varieties take years.
What traits do
The main GM trait groups
GM traits fall into five main groups. In Nigeria, the regulator has published notices on insect-resistant cowpea and TELA maize.
But a trait solves one named problem. A Bt cowpea still needs weeding and proper drying. Always ask: which crop, which trait, which event, and which country?
Audit a claim
Environment: insects, weeds, wild plants
Law: approved, labelled, regulated?
Most confusion comes from mixing up kinds of question. Each needs its own evidence.

For example, Halima in Kano got a voice note from a cousin. She wrote down each claim and found 4 claims, 4 different types, and 0 sources named. The legal claim she could check that day on the NBMA website.
Key points
Remember
A gene is a recipe, usually for a protein
A GMO is defined by how its DNA was changed
Regulators approve a named event
Sort claims into four types
To remember. A gene is a recipe. A GMO is defined by the method. Approvals name a specific event. Never plant seed of unknown origin. And sort every claim by its type.

Why this matters
Three big questions
Is GM food safe to eat?
What happens in the field and the farm account?
Who decides what may be planted?
This module looks at the evidence behind three big questions. First, is GM food safe to eat?
Second, what happens in the field and in the farm account book?
And third, who decides what may be planted in Nigeria?
Six things WHO says are assessed
Toxicity of the new protein
Key nutrients and natural toxins
Nutritional effects

Scientists ask a narrow question: is this food, from this event, as safe as the conventional food it replaces? Assessors check whether the new protein could be toxic, and whether it could cause an allergy.
They measure key nutrients and natural toxins, and check that the inserted gene stays stable over generations.
And they look for nutritional effects, and for any change nobody planned. Eating DNA is not a risk in itself. Digestion breaks it down.
Worked example
Reading a side-by-side comparison
Worry about differences that are large or outside the normal range.
GM line: 24.1 g protein per 100 g
Comparator: 23.5 g
Difference: 0.6 g, about 2.6 percent
Normal range: 20.0 to 28.0 g
The GM plant is grown beside a conventional comparator. In a practice example, a GM cowpea has 24.1 grams of protein per 100 grams, and the comparator 23.5.
The difference is 0.6 grams, about 2.6 percent.
Ordinary varieties range from 20.0 to 28.0 grams, so this is normal. But if a natural anti-nutrient were 40 percent higher and outside the range, it would need explanation before approval.
Read it carefully
What WHO does and does not say
WHO says
Approved GM foods passed assessment
Not likely to present health risks
Assess each food case by case
WHO does not say
WHO states that GM foods on the international market have passed safety assessments and are not likely to present risks for human health.
Read it carefully. It covers foods that passed assessment. It does not say every possible GM food is safe. That is exactly why regulation exists.
In the field
A refuge slows resistance
Use the refuge size in your own seed's stewardship guide.
2 hectares = 20,000 square metres
Refuge, 20 percent: 4,000 square metres
Bt cowpea: 16,000 square metres
Strip along a 100 m side: 40 m deep
Insects evolve. If Bt plants kill almost every pod borer, rare resistant survivors mate and the trait wears out. A refuge of non-Bt plants nearby keeps the population susceptible.
For example, Ngozi farms 2 hectares in Benue.
Suppose her leaflet says 20 percent refuge. That is 4,000 square metres.
She plants 16,000 square metres of Bt cowpea, and a strip 40 metres deep of non-Bt cowpea. One farmer who skips the refuge weakens the trait for every neighbour.

Economic claims cut both ways. Here is an illustrative table. The prices are for practice only.

Safety first
Everyday safety still applies
Mould and aflatoxin grow in badly dried maize and groundnuts. Store off the floor in clean bags.
Gloves, long sleeves, boots, face covering. Never spray into the wind. Keep children away.
Never eat seed treated with chemicals. Never store chemicals in food or drink containers.
GM or not, everyday hazards remain. Dry grain well, because mould and aflatoxin grow in damp maize and groundnuts.
A Bt crop controls only its target pests. If you still spray, wear protection, never spray into the wind, and observe the waiting period on the label before harvest.
And never eat seed treated with chemicals.
Who decides
From world rules to Nigeria's NBMA
Check the regulator's own notice, and note its date.
Cartagena Protocol, adopted 29 January 2000
Codex: food safety assessment guidance
Nigeria: NBMA, under the 2015 Act
Release applications go on public display
Send a specific, polite comment in time
No single world authority approves GM crops. The Cartagena Protocol protects biodiversity and lets countries get information before agreeing to imports. Codex guides food safety assessment.
In Nigeria, the regulator is the National Biosafety Management Agency, NBMA, under an Act signed in April 2015.
Applications to release a GMO go on public display. For example, the GM cowpea application in April 2023 was displayed for 21 days.
Name the application, say who you are, and ask clear questions, such as how refuge rules will be explained to smallholders. Set your own deadline 3 days early, and keep a copy.
Key points
Remember
Safety is judged product by product
Differences inside the normal range are not a concern alone
A refuge keeps Bt working
Compare costs with your own farm numbers
NBMA decides; comment during public display
To remember. Safety is judged product by product, against a comparator. Follow your refuge rules. Use your own numbers for costs. And check NBMA's notices before you repeat a claim about the law.

Why this matters
From knowledge to leadership
Test any claim with one method
Run a calm, respectful conversation
Build your three-part project
This module turns your knowledge into community leadership. The aim is not to win arguments. It is to reach a fair verdict you can explain.
You will learn a scoring method for any claim, a plan for a balanced community conversation, and the final project that brings it together.
The method
Five questions, scored 0 to 2
First, rewrite the claim as one clear sentence. Vague claims like GMOs are poison name no crop or effect.
Second, the type: food safety, environment, economics or law. Does the evidence match? A seed price cannot prove a health danger.
Third, the source. A regulator, WHO or a named study scores 2. An anonymous forward scores 0.
Fourth, can you follow the evidence to the original document? And fifth, is it about an approved product in your country, and current? Add the scores for a total out of 10.
Worked example
Chioma scores two WhatsApp claims
8 to 10 credible. 4 to 7 check more. 0 to 3 do not repeat it.
Claim 1: GM foods cause cancer, a doctor said so
Scores 1, 0, 0, 0, 0: total 1 out of 10
Claim 2: GM cowpea will end hunger in Nigeria
Scores 1, 0, 0, 0, 2: total 3 out of 10
For example, Chioma, a nurse in Port Harcourt, scores two messages from her church group. The first names no crop, no evidence and an unnamed doctor. It scores 1 out of 10.
The second is in favour of GMOs. It came from a seed advert with no yield or price data. It scores 3. Hunger also depends on prices, storage, income and conflict.
Both score 3 or less, so she forwards neither. She posts one calm message with WHO's statement and a link to NBMA's website. Score a claim you like with the same care as one you dislike.
Warning signs
Anti-GMO
All GMOs are poison
Your children will be infertile
Scientists have proved...
Pro-GMO
GMOs have no risks at all
This seed will end hunger
Studies show...
Watch for absolute words, fear language and no checkable source.
The same signs appear on the other side: no risks at all, miracle language, and studies nobody can find.
Protect your money
Be careful with anyone selling a kit to detect GMO in your food at home.
A remedy to remove GMO from your body is a warning sign. Do not send money.
Unlabelled seed sold as a new GM variety outside a registered dealer. Ask NBMA first.
Scammers use these fears and hopes. Be careful with anyone selling a test kit to detect GMO in your food.
Or a remedy to remove GMO from your body.
Or seed claiming to be an approved GM variety outside a registered dealer. Do not send money or personal details. Ask NBMA or your extension office first.
Leading a session
Grace's 30-minute session
Listen first. Give the group more time than you take.
Welcome and ground rules: 3 minutes
Collect what people heard: 7 minutes
Sort concerns into four types: 5 minutes
Share checked facts: 6 minutes
Discuss open questions: 6 minutes
Agree next steps: 3 minutes

Facts alone rarely change minds. People care about their children's health, their money and their land. For example, Grace leads a 25-member cooperative in Plateau. She welcomes people, then writes what they have heard on a flip chart.
Together they sort concerns into the four types. Many arguments disappear once people see they are different questions.
She reads WHO's sentence aloud exactly as written, and shows NBMA's website. Then farmers speak first on open questions like seed cost and refuge rules.
It adds up to 30 minutes, with 21 for the group to talk and only 6 for facts. If you do not know an answer, say, I do not know yet, I will ask and report back.
Final project
Your three short documents

Audience, one message, channel, date, and a number you can count.
Your project has three parts. Part A: your country's law and regulator, with dates. Mark anything you could not confirm as not confirmed.
Part B: one real claim, scored, with a verdict that says what the claim says, what the evidence shows, and what is still uncertain.
Part C: an outreach plan. For example, Aisha in Kaduna held a session where 32 of 40 members came, which is 80 percent.
Key points
Remember
What, type, source, evidence, here and now
0 to 3 means do not repeat it
Warning signs appear on both sides
Listen first, sort, then share checked facts
Recheck the regulator, because approvals change

To remember. Score claims with five questions, and do not repeat a low score. Watch for warning signs on both sides. Listen before you explain. And recheck the regulator's website, because approvals change.
